1.pericope_label: by what authority doest thou these things?

schools.summary: Theophylact reads the counter-question as an exposure of a settled habit — a people who had refused Isaiah and then John.

Eusebius supplies the legal grievance, that by Moses only the tribe of Levi might teach and keep the sacred buildings, and narrows the counter-question to the source of John's baptism rather than John's parentage.

Augustine explains the vague opening as Luke declining to follow the days in order; Bede takes the challenge as a charge of demonic power, and defends the counter-question as making the questioners condemn themselves.

Robertson dates the scene to the Tuesday, reads the delegation as Sadducees and Pharisees together, and glosses the verbs for their sudden approach, their reckoning and the stoning they feared; Lightfoot identifies the elders as the lay members of the Sanhedrin; Ellicott marks Luke's stoning as sharper than the general fear in the other Gospels.
Gill counts the days from the entry into Jerusalem and says plainly that their profession of ignorance was an untruth.
Henry hears both surprise and intimidation in the approach, and takes the interruption of the preaching as the point.
Clarke agrees on the Tuesday before the passover.

themes: tell us, by what authority doest thou these things?
the baptism of John: from heaven, or of men?
neither tell I you by what authority

9.pericope_label: the vineyard let out, and the servants sent

schools.summary: Theophylact makes each hearer both vineyard and husbandman, and reads the long absence as indulgence that leaves obstinacy less excusable; Chrysostom explains the sending of the Son after the servants as accommodation to human weakness.
Eusebius marks the difference from Isaiah — this parable is aimed at the cultivators, not the vineyard; Cyril dates the withdrawal of the visible presence from Sinai.

Ambrose identifies the vineyard from Isaiah as the house of Israel; Augustine notes that Luke alone records that the parable was spoken to the people as well as the rulers; Bede names the three sendings as Moses, David and the prophets.
Gill takes the parable as addressed to both crowd and council, with the priests chiefly in view.

themes: a certain man planted a vineyard
he sent a servant, and they beat him
the fruit of the vineyard demanded

13.pericope_label: the beloved son sent, and killed

schools.summary: Theophylact denies that the deliberation springs from ignorance — the doubtful form of words preserves human freedom and forestalls the plea that refusal was inevitable — and reads the killing outside the vineyard as delivery to Pilate and the Gentiles; Basil takes the announced sentence as mercy, God not punishing in secret.
Cyril has every device of human help tried on a people no whit healed before something greater is added.

Bede insists the rulers acted from envy and not ignorance, and turns the parable inward on the baptised; Ambrose reads the coming of the lord of the vineyard as the coming of the Son, in whom the Father's majesty is present; Augustine resolves the difference from Matthew by dividing the crowd.
Henry hears the calculation in their speech — kill the servants and more come, kill the son and none is left — and marks the change of voice from servant to Son.

debates.question: Who says "he will destroy those husbandmen"?
positions: Theophylact: the Jews said it first, then recoiled with "God forbid" once they saw the point
Augustine: the crowd was mixed, one part giving the true verdict and another protesting

themes: I will send my beloved son
this is the heir: let us kill him
he shall come and destroy those husbandmen

17.pericope_label: the stone which the builders rejected

schools.summary: Theophylact dates the rejection to their sentence that this man is not of God.

Eusebius explains the metaphor by the incarnation — a stone cut without hands, neither silver nor gold because he came lowly; Cyril reads the corner as Jew and Gentile made one man, and distinguishes the ruin of their souls from the ruin of their nation.

Bede takes the corner as a question about how else the prophecy could be fulfilled, and grades the two fates by degree, leaving room for penitence; he also sees the rulers proving the parable true by resenting it.

Robertson calls the glance piercing and notes Luke's time-marker for the council's anger; Ellicott says the verb means a fixed gaze, and observes that the verse about the stone stands in every manuscript of Luke though not of Matthew.
Gill guards the first clause, since falling on Christ can also be said of faith.
Wesley thinks the look was meant to sharpen their attention.

debates.question: What are the two fates in v.18?
positions: Cyril: the ruin of their souls in taking offence, and the ruin of the nation in captivity
Bede: degrees of guilt, the believing sinner shaken and preserved, the denier crushed

themes: the stone which the builders rejected
broken, and ground to powder
they feared the people

20.pericope_label: the spies, and the question about tribute

schools.summary: Bede sets out the fork the question was meant to be — say yes and the crowd hears a man putting the nation under the yoke, say no and the guards arrest a rebel.

Robertson explains the vocabulary of insidious watching and of hired liers-in-wait, and notes that the aim of delivering him to the governor is stated by Luke alone; Ellicott traces the phrase about accepting no person to Paul.
Gill locates the whole weight of the question in the two words Luke adds — whether we, Abraham's seed, may pay an heathen emperor.
Henry names the strategy — failing to be his judges they would be his prosecutors — and refuses to let the pretence of justice pass unremarked.
Clarke traces the word for spies to a root meaning to set in ambush and cites Josephus using it of a man bribed for a purpose; Wesley glosses the pretence as men of tender conscience.

themes: spies, which should feign themselves just men
is it lawful for us to give tribute unto Caesar?
that they might deliver him unto the governor

23.pericope_label: render unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's

schools.summary: Theophylact fastens on the verb — not give but render, because it is a debt — and turns it round on the reason and understanding God has given; Titus of Bostra sums the reply in a sentence, that God asks not money but faith.

Cyril denies that the question about the image betrays ignorance, and identifies the Caesar as Tiberius; Origen finds two images in man, one from God and one contracted from the enemy, so that rendering to Caesar means casting the earthly one away.
Bede specifies what the second half claims — tithes, firstfruits, offerings and sacrifices; Ambrose draws the moral that no one can be the Lord's who has not first renounced the world.
Robertson notes that the word for their failure means they lacked the strength for it; Ellicott hears an undesigned echo of the boy in the temple whose answers astonished the doctors.
Henry divides the two spheres — submission to the civil power in civil things, worship reserved to God, who alone may ask for the heart.
Wesley limits the defeat to what happened before the people, the council managing it later without the crowd.

outliers: Origen alone reads the coin allegorically, finding in man two images — one received from God at his making and one contracted from the enemy by sin.
themes: whose image and superscription hath it?
render unto God the things which be God's
they marvelled at his answer, and held their peace

27.pericope_label: the Sadducees and the seven brothers

schools.summary: Theophylact explains that imagining the future life as carnal is what made the sect think the doctrine impossible, so that they invented a story to ridicule it.
Origen states the denial precisely — not the resurrection only, but the survival of the soul — and notes that they chose their moment.

Bede distinguishes the two sects by their names and calls the story a base fable devised to convict the orthodox of folly; Ambrose reads the levirate letter as killing where the Spirit gives charity, and allegorises the woman as the synagogue with seven husbands.
Gill dates the approach to the same day as the tribute question.
Henry draws out what the denial costs — no world of spirits and no recompense, so that all religion falls — and describes the method of loading a truth with difficulties.

debates.question: What do the seven husbands signify?
positions: Ambrose: the synagogue, barren of spiritual offspring through reading the precept carnally
Bede: the reprobate, fruitless through the whole week-long course of the world

themes: which deny that there is any resurrection
seven brethren, and the woman died also
whose wife of them is she?

34.pericope_label: equal unto the angels, and the children of God

schools.summary: Theophylact reads the whole answer as denying any fleshly manner of life in the resurrection, and explains the title of sons of God from the resurrection itself, in which there is no coming together, no womb and no birth.
Cyril grounds the comparison with the angels in their being created rather than propagated.

Augustine gives the chain — marriage for children, children for succession, succession because of death — and compares the Word that has all it has at once with speech built of passing syllables; Bede cautions that sinners rise too, the elect being named only to draw the hearers on.

Robertson notes that the word for equal to the angels is found nowhere else in the New Testament; Ellicott marks the contrast of the two ages as Luke's own and reads death and marriage as correlative facts in the government of the world.
Gill is careful how a man comes to be accounted worthy — not by merit but through the righteousness of the Messiah.
Clarke and Wesley both explain marriage in this world by the need to repair the waste that death makes.

themes: the children of this world marry, and are given in marriage
neither can they die any more
equal unto the angels

37.pericope_label: the God of Abraham, and of the living

schools.summary: Theophylact rests the argument on the tense — I was is said of what is dead and gone, I am of the living; Chrysostom takes the divine name as affection rather than limitation, the master taking his name from the servant.
Bede notes the order of the proof, souls surviving death first and the resurrection of bodies after, and explains the choice of Moses by what the Sadducees would accept.
Lightfoot quotes the rabbinic story in which Moses, short of ten righteous men, asks whether the dead live and then names the patriarchs.

Calvin locates the force not in the idiom but in the promise: God offers himself as our God only on condition of taking us for his people, and no man is a father without children or a king without a people.
Wesley states in a line that God cannot properly be called the God of any who have utterly perished; Clarke adds the Maccabean saying that those who die for God live unto God.

themes: even Moses shewed at the bush
he is not a God of the dead, but of the living
for all live unto him

schools.summary: Robertson identifies the speakers as Pharisees pleased to see the Pentateuch turned against the Sadducees, and reads the silence as courage vanished; Ellicott takes the words for the better sort of Pharisee and treats Luke's omission of the great commandment as a proof of his independence.

Calvin credits the confession to providence rather than goodwill — envy at the prospect of a Sadducee victory, and a secret divine constraint — and finds it a wonder of the age that the resurrection could be proved so ably out of the Law; Gill notes that these scribes already held the doctrine.
Henry uses the testimony as evidence about the witnesses, and observes that many who call themselves Christians come short even of it.
Clarke reads the silence as a decision not to risk being confounded again; Wesley limits it, since one of the scribes did ask immediately afterwards.

outliers: Ellicott alone raises Luke's omission of the question about the great commandment, which he cannot account for except by supposing Luke did not know of it.
themes: Master, thou hast well said
they durst not ask him any question at all
his adversaries commend his answer

schools.summary: Theophylact marks the manner — the Godhead proclaimed neither incautiously nor boastfully, but by a question left for the hearers to finish; Chrysostom compresses the puzzle into a sentence, David being father and servant both.
Cyril reads the seat at the right hand as proof of heavenly glory, equal throne meaning equal majesty, and turns the same question against those who divide one Son into two.

Ambrose distinguishes what is blamed — not calling him David's son, but refusing to believe him Son of God — and denies that sitting at the right hand implies either honour gained or dignity lost; Augustine warns against imagining a posture, the right hand being the power received by the Man taken up into God.

Robertson observes that the words treat David as the author of the psalm and that its two natures are the problem which troubled the rabbis and troubles critics still; Lightfoot notes that the later Jewish evasions — Abraham, David, Hezekiah — had not yet been invented.
Henry states the apparent contradiction and gives the resolution: as God David's Lord, as man David's son, at once the root and the offspring of David.
Clarke takes the footstool at full weight, the enemies not merely humbled but wholly subjected to the Christ they were about to crucify.

themes: how say they that Christ is David's son?
the LORD said unto my Lord, sit thou on my right hand
David therefore calleth him Lord

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains why the warning comes now — argument from the prophets silences men as miracles did not; Theophylact adds that disciples about to be sent out must not imitate the pride they have just watched, and names the aggravation, that a show of prayer makes virtue the cover for the sin.
Cyril names the two faults exactly: the love of vainglory and the love of gain.

Bede distinguishes the dignity from the love of it, gives two reasons for being warned rather than merely disapproving, and describes how money was got from the sick and the troubled by men passing for protectors at the judgment.
Robertson notes the genitive absolute placing the warning while all the people were listening; Lightfoot documents the long robes from the rabbis.
Gill sets the two verses against each other, the one exposing pride and the other avarice.
Clarke calls a bad example backed by the majesty of religion a subtle poison, and refuses to let the charge be used by one party against another.

outliers: Clarke turns the warning away from partisan use, insisting such ministers are found in the separated bodies as much as in the churches they left.
themes: which desire to walk in long robes
which devour widows' houses, and for a shew make long prayers
the same shall receive greater damnation
